current_activity: redesignated XVIII Airborne Corps at Ogbourne St George with the 82nd and 101st Airborne Divisions
notes: Event date: Wikipedia: XVIII Corps deployed to Europe on 17 August and became XVIII Airborne Corps on 25 August 1944 at Ogbourne St George (assuming command of the 82nd and 101st Airborne Divisions). Event definition: redesignation of the same headquarters (II Armored Corps, 1942; XVIII Corps, 9 October 1943; XVIII Airborne Corps, 25 August 1944; see units.csv note). Relationship: the CMH tables assign the 82nd and 101st Airborne Divisions to the corps from 12 August, when it was still the XVIII Corps and still in the United States; it is not an airborne corps headquarters in Europe before 25 August. The corps was assigned to First Allied Airborne Army (CMH tables, not distinguished as assigned or attached). It was in England during Market Garden, where British I Airborne Corps held operational control of the US airborne divisions.

current_activity: Ridgway opens the corps command post near the 82nd Airborne and the corps becomes operational under First Army
notes: Event date: 19 December 1944 (Ardennes p343: "the following morning" after the 82nd's night move of 18 December, Ridgway, who had resumed command of the airborne corps, opened his corps command post near that of the 82d; the First Army, then at Chaudfontaine, gave him the directive making the corps operational later that morning). Event definition: the XVIII Airborne Corps headquarters, in England until now, takes command of the 82nd Airborne and, soon after, the 7th Armored, 3rd Armored and 30th Divisions on First Army's left; the row dates the first operational day, not the corps arrival in France. Relationship: First Army operational_control from 19 December (directive making the corps operational); the corps stays assigned to the First Allied Airborne Army (CMH tables). Location: The Green Book puts the corps command post near the 82nd's; the atlas lists the 82nd command post at Habiémont on 19 December and the corps at Manhay on 20 December. Habiémont is the documented place of the 82nd's command post, used as an inference for the corps command post; no source names the corps command post for 19 December (the first atlas entry for the corps is Manhay on 20 December). Coordinates: Wikipedia (fr): Habiémont. Event support: high (Green Book narrative). Location support: moderate (the place is inferred from the neighbouring command post, not named for the corps).

current_activity: Varsity: commands the 6th British and 17th US Airborne Divisions in the drop on the Diersfordter Forst
notes: Event date: 24 March 1945, shortly before 10:00 (CMH, The Last Offensive, ch. 14, p. 309: the airborne armada appears over the Rhine). Event definition: The corps headquarters, attached to the British Second Army for the Rhine crossing, controls the 6th British and 17th US Airborne Divisions, which drop and land north-west of Wesel to seize the high ground of the Diersfordter Forst; General Ridgway and his staff do not take part in the drop but are in position on the west bank of the Rhine (MacDonald, ch. 14, pp. 298-300, 310; Ellis, vol. II, p. 285). After the crossing the corps is relieved of its British units, which pass to the British Second Army, and its headquarters shifts to the US First Army to take command of the units facing the Sieg River in the reduction of the Ruhr Pocket, attacking under First Army on 6 April (MacDonald, ch. 16, pp. 357, 362, 365; the first plan is of 29 March, the shift is read as 2 April, see the relations). Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and CMH, MacDonald, The Last Offensive). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 285: "Second Army: XII Corps (Assault)"; "XVIIT U.S. Airborne Corps (Assault): 6th British and 17th U.S. Airborne Divisions"; MacDonald, The Last Offensive, ch. 14, p. 298: "As of 9 March, when Montgomery issued his basic order, plans for using the two airborne divisions that were attached to the Second Army and headquarters of the XVIII Airborne Corps that controlled them still were indefinite"; p. 299: "was to be made by the XVIII Airborne Corps under General Ridgway, employing the British 6th Airborne Division and the U.S. 17th"; p. 300: "to seize high ground crowned by the Diersfordter Forst northwest of Wesel"; p. 309: "shortly before 1000 on 24 March the steady drone of hundreds of aircraft motors began to emerge from the west"; p. 310: "the commander, General Ridgway, and staff of the XVIII Airborne Corps did not participate in the airborne assault but were already in position on the west bank of the Rhine"; ch. 16, p. 357: "British units within the corps passing to the British Second Army"; p. 362: "shifted to the First Army and assumed command of those units facing northward along the Sieg River"; p. 365: "The III Corps began to attack on 5 April, the XVIII Airborne Corps the next day". Location: Diersfordt, North Rhine-Westphalia (existing place PL0437), the village at the Diersfordter Forst, the corps objective with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the objective of the corps (the village of Diersfordt at the Diersfordter Forst), not the position of the corps headquarters, which CMH puts on the west bank of the Rhine (p. 310) without naming a place; the precision is 10 km. Location support: CMH names the Diersfordter Forst north-west of Wesel as the corps objective; Ellis lists the corps and its two divisions for the assault (p. 285). Commander: Maj. Gen. Matthew B. Ridgway, commanding the XVIII Airborne Corps (CMH, The Last Offensive, ch. 14). Context: Review (British Batch 2 follow-up, 28 October 2026): the row is the one US claim written in this follow-up. It gives the corps the Second Army as its operational parent for Operation Plunder-Varsity; it is 0.3 because the point is the objective, not the headquarters. The validator gives one expected warning for this row (it is not an error): the row lists the US First Army relation (CR0922, operational_control) with a start of 2 April 1945, after the row date; the row states that start (and the end of the Second Army attachment, CR0921, on 1 April) from MacDonald, ch. 16, pp. 357, 362 and 365, because no other row of the corps exists in April 1945 to state them and the corps would otherwise have no army above it after the Plunder attachment; both dates are inferred values and say so in the relation notes.
